newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs set new highs, shake off land remedy worries.
newsitem.headline: JGBs set new highs, shake off land remedy worries.

text.p: Japanese government bonds (JGBs) climbed to record highs on Tuesday, shaking off worries that the government may soon come up with concrete measures to rejuvenate the country's stagnant land market, traders said.
Massive JGB selling was prompted late on Monday by speculation the government would announce steps to raise land liquidity as early as on Tuesday, traders said.
However, when that did not happen on Tuesday, a wave of short covering was set off, driving up JGB prices to record high levels.
The benchmark 182nd 10-year JGB yield fell to an all-time low of 2.310 percent in late Tokyo trading on Tuesday.
A lack of land liquidity is at the core of the nation's bad loan problem, not just for the ailing banking sector but for a wide swathe of corporate Japan.
Revitalised land transactions would raise the prospect of a healthy economic recovery, giving the Bank of Japan (BOJ) leeway to tighten its credit grip, traders said.
In February, Finance Ministry officials said a government panel was considering using funds already set aside in the next year's state budget to buy land formerly owned by troubled financial firms.
They said the proposal would help ease the land liquidity crisis, but so far no concrete plans have been disclosed.
But traders remained sceptical that the government can come up with a quick fix for the land problem that would pour cold water on the current JGB bull-run.

"Any short-term government step, including on land, would be to lend support to (Tokyo) stock prices at the end-March corporate book closings," said Yasunari Ueno, chief market economist at Fuji Securities Co Ltd.
But any announcement on the land transaction plans will probably be later this month or close to March 31 to maximise the positive effect on the stock market, he added.
Traders said unless the government shows wholehearted commitment to resolving the land liquidity problem, JGBs will remain bullish.

"The central bank would not mind further falls in long-term rates, as it is more concerned about a drag on the economy from contractionary fiscal policies, such as higher taxes, than the chance of import-led inflation due to a weak yen," Ueno said.
The BOJ's Research and Statistics Department said recently that Japan's private-sector demand is firming, but adverse effects of the April 1 consumption tax hike cannot be avoided.
It also said there is little concern over higher import prices directly leading to a rise in wholesale prices because the nation's supply-demand situation was not that tight yet.
The go-ahead signals have sent JGBs sailing forward into uncharted water.

"We previously thought the bond price would peak in the April-June quarter, but it appears the rally has already taken off," said Tadao Sakashima, assistant general manager in the bond department of Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.
The earlier-than-expected JGB rally was partly a reflection of earlier bad timing by portfolio managers.
Many of them failed to boost their JGB weightings in the first half of 1996/97 as they wrongly assumed an early credit tightening by the BOJ in mid-1996.
Other bullish factors include much-smaller-than-expected municipal bond issues for the current fiscal year, and plans by cash-rich agricultural banks to boost their JGB holdings.
